claims.text: Repeated arc melting of WTaTiVZr produces grain refinement.
Repeated arc melting of WTaTiVZr produces uniformly distributed nanoscale secondary phases.
The secondary phases occur both along grain boundaries and within grains.
The nanoscale secondary phases pin grain boundaries.
The nanoscale secondary phases pin dislocations and restrict dislocation motion.
Grain refinement and dispersed secondary phases delay crack initiation and propagation.
Restricting dislocation motion and delaying cracking increase high-temperature plasticity.
Restricting dislocation motion and delaying cracking improve high-temperature toughness.
Repeatedly remelted WTaTiVZr will exhibit significantly greater high-temperature plastic strain than singly melted pure tungsten.
Repeatedly remelted WTaTiVZr will exhibit significantly greater high-temperature toughness than singly melted pure tungsten.
The predicted mechanical-property improvements arise from stabilization by the refined microstructure.
The proposed mechanism applies at temperatures above 1000°C under dynamic, high-stress loading representative of fusion plasma-facing service.
The beneficial effect may diminish at lower temperatures.
The beneficial effect may diminish when radiation-induced damage dominates microstructural evolution.
Irradiation and chemical interactions with plasma may introduce effects not captured by the proposed comparison.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes the outcome to repeated remelting, but the comparison changes both composition and processing history: repeatedly remelted WTaTiVZr is compared with singly melted pure tungsten. Without a singly melted WTaTiVZr control, the proposed experiment cannot isolate repeated remelting from alloy-composition effects.
The initial-state field identifies singly melted WTaTiVZr as an available starting condition, but the falsification design omits this unperturbed same-alloy baseline and instead uses pure tungsten.
